precepts.text: And it was the preparation of the passover, and about the sixth hour: and he saith unto the Jews, Behold your King! But they cried out, Away with him, away with him, crucify him. Pilate saith unto them, Shall I crucify your King? The chief priests answered, We have no king but Caesar. Then delivered he him therefore unto them to be crucified. And they took Jesus, and led him away. That is how he was taken from prison and from judgment.
precepts.point: He was taken from prison and from judgment: and who shall declare his generation? for he was cut off out of the land of the living: for the transgression of my people was he stricken. Now, we might think that Christ does not understand what we are going through. I am going to show you that Christ knows perfectly well what we are going through. The whole chapter is talking about Christ, but I want to focus on verse 8. He was taken from prison and from judgment. He was cut off out of the land of the living: that is when he was crucified.

note.label: Prison House of Shadows

precepts.why:
We might think that Christ doesn't understand what we are going through. Isaiah 53 shows that Christ knows perfectly well what we are going through. The whole chapter is talking about Christ, and verse 8 says: “He was taken from prison and from judgment.” How?

John shows it. “And from thenceforth Pilate sought to release him: but the Jews cried out, saying, If thou let this man go, thou art not Cesar’s friend.” Pilate “brought Jesus forth, and sat down in the judgment seat in a place that is called the Pavement, but in the Hebrew, Gabbatha.”

“And it was the preparation of the passover, and about the sixth hour: and he saith unto the Jews, Behold your King! But they cried out, Away with him, away with him, crucify him. Pilate saith unto them, Shall I crucify your King? The chief priests answered, We have no king but Cesar. Then delivered he him therefore unto them to be crucified. And they took Jesus, and led him away.”

That is how he was taken from prison and from judgment: bound, set before the judgment seat, rejected by his own for Caesar, and led away. The one who was taken from prison is the one who comes to preach to our people, who are in the prison house today.

precepts.text: A seed shall serve him; it shall be accounted to the Lord for a generation. They shall come, and shall declare his righteousness unto a people that shall be born, that he hath done this. To declare means to teach. To declare means to preach. They shall come and shall declare his righteousness. That is us, you and me. Unto a people that shall be born. That is us.
precepts.point: He was taken from prison and from judgment: and who shall declare his generation? for he was cut off out of the land of the living: for the transgression of my people was he stricken. Now, we might think that Christ does not understand what we are going through. I am going to show you that Christ knows perfectly well what we are going through. The whole chapter is talking about Christ, but I want to focus on verse 8. He was taken from prison and from judgment. He was cut off out of the land of the living: that is when he was crucified.

note.label: Prison House of Shadows

precepts.why:
“and who shall declare his generation?” David answers: “A seed shall serve him; it shall be accounted to the Lord for a generation. They shall come, and shall declare his righteousness unto a people that shall be born, that he hath done this.”

To declare means to teach. To declare means to preach. They shall come and shall declare his righteousness: that's us, you and me. Unto a people that shall be born: that's us too.

So the question Isaiah asks is answered by a seed that serves him and is accounted to the Lord for a generation. Christ was cut off out of the land of the living, but his generation is declared by those who come after, teaching and preaching his righteousness to our people that he hath done this.

precepts.text: And after threescore and two weeks shall Messiah be cut off, but not for himself: and the people of the prince that shall come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary; and the end thereof shall be with a flood, and unto the end of the war desolations are determined. Shall Messiah, that is Christ, be cut off, but not for himself. He did not die for himself. And the people of the prince that shall come: Rome.
precepts.point: He was taken from prison and from judgment: and who shall declare his generation? for he was cut off out of the land of the living: for the transgression of my people was he stricken. Now, we might think that Christ does not understand what we are going through. I am going to show you that Christ knows perfectly well what we are going through. The whole chapter is talking about Christ, but I want to focus on verse 8. He was taken from prison and from judgment. He was cut off out of the land of the living: that is when he was crucified.

note.label: Prison House of Shadows

precepts.why:
“for he was cut off out of the land of the living”: that is when he was crucified. Daniel prophesied it: “And after threescore and two weeks shall Messiah be cut off, but not for himself.” Messiah, that's Christ, is cut off, but not for himself. He didn't die for himself; Isaiah says, “for the transgression of my people was he stricken.”

“and the people of the prince that shall come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary; and the end thereof shall be with a flood, and unto the end of the war desolations are determined.” The people of the prince that shall come is Rome.

So the same Rome that dominated Israel when Christ was cut off came and destroyed the city and the sanctuary. Christ was cut off for the transgression of his people, and desolations were determined upon the city by the hand of Rome.

precepts.text: Yet it pleased the Lord to bruise him; when thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin. His soul, not a goat or a lamb; and they ignored that too.
precepts.point: Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross. The subject has not changed: they were beguiling Israel to go back to animal sacrifice, and they did not understand that animal sacrifice was a symbol of what Christ would do for us.

note.label: Deceived by Enticing Words: Colossians 2

precepts.why:
“Yet it pleased the Lord to bruise him; he hath put him to grief: when thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin.” It pleased the Lord to bruise him, Christ. See that: his soul an offering for sin, not a goat or a lamb.

The scribes said, well, we're just going to ignore that; we're dealing with goats, lambs and oxen, and to hell with all that mumbo gumbo y'all coming with. But the prophet said the offering for sin would be his soul, and then “he shall see his seed, he shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of the Lord shall prosper in his hand.”

That is why the ordinances of animal sacrifice could be blotted out. The offering for sin that Isaiah saw was Christ himself.

precepts.text: Surely he hath borne our griefs and carried our sorrows; he was wounded for our transgressions, bruised for our iniquities, the chastisement of our peace was upon him, and with his stripes we are healed. All we like sheep, the house of Israel, have gone astray, and the Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all. He was cut off out of the land of the living for the transgression of my people; not all people, not the good nations, my people, and Isaiah was an Israelite. Show me where the Old Testament changed that and Christ died a second time for heathens. By his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many, for he shall bear their iniquities; he bare the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors, an intercessor who dies in your place. There is no Isaiah 53 part two for other nations.
precepts.point: It was not written for his sake alone, but for us also, to whom it shall be imputed, if we believe on him that raised up Jesus our Lord from the dead, who was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification. Israel was accustomed to sacrificing; Paul says fine, but acknowledge Christ first, because if you put your faith in the animal and the temple falls, you have condemned yourself by default with no animal, no priest, and no temple.

note.label: Navigating Through Paul's Letters: Walk Through of Romans 5

precepts.why:
Paul says Christ “was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification.” Our offences: whose? Isaiah 53 shows who Christ was delivered for. “Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows”: this is Isaiah speaking of his people. “But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.” Maybe you are thinking that is everybody. Keep reading.

“All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.” Like sheep of the house of Israel. The us is the sheep. “He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth”; he did not say one word. Then: “for he was cut off out of the land of the living: for the transgression of my people was he stricken.” Not all people, not all nations, not the good nations, not the not-so-bad ones. My people. And Isaiah was an Israelite. Now you know who the our is, who the all is, who the we is.

All the apologists online have to do is show us in the Old Testament where this changed and Christ came back a second time and died for heathens. Show where Isaiah says, oh yeah, I almost forgot the other nations. Peter said the unlearned and unstable wrest Paul’s letters as they do the other scriptures, but this is what Paul got it from.

“By his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many; for he shall bear their iniquities.” Many who? Israelites; the thought has not changed. “He bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.” An intercessor is a mediator, someone who steps in and dies in your place. There is no Isaiah 53 part two for the other nations. Abraham believed without the works of sacrifice, and so must we: faith in the one delivered for our offences.

precepts.text: He was wounded for our transgressions and brought as a lamb to the slaughter; he was cut off for the transgression of my people, and his soul was made an offering for sin.
precepts.point: Isaiah 53 cannot be speaking of David, who was already dead in Isaiah's day; it speaks of Jesus Christ, cut off out of the land of the living for the transgression of the people, the ultimate sacrifice.

note.label: Numbers 29: The Feasts of the Seventh Month

precepts.why:
We fast on the day of atonement without the sacrifices, because the atonement is now Christ. “But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.” The Lord laid on him the iniquity of us all, just as the priest laid the sins of the nation on the sacrifice of Leviticus 16.

“He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth.” He was brought as a lamb to the slaughter, the ultimate sacrifice; that is why the veil rent in two when he died.

“for he was cut off out of the land of the living: for the transgression of my people was he stricken.” This cannot be speaking of David, who was already dead in Isaiah's day; it speaks of Jesus Christ, cut off out of the land of the living for the transgression of the people. “Yet it pleased the Lord to bruise him; he hath put him to grief: when thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed, he shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of the Lord shall prosper in his hand.” His soul was made an offering for sin, the sin offering of atonement.

precepts.text: Yet it pleased the Lord to bruise him, when thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin; his soul was made a sin offering, and he shall see his seed and prolong his days.
precepts.point: I am poured out like water and all my bones are out of joint; my strength is dried up, they pierced my hands and my feet, I may tell all my bones. His soul was made a sin offering; they pierced his hands and feet as they did to Christ, and because he was already dead none of his bones were broken, so the prophecy that he could tell all his bones was fulfilled.

note.label: Psalm 22: The Prophecy of Christ on the Cross

precepts.why:
“For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet. I may tell all my bones”. Isaiah tells what was happening: “Yet it pleased the Lord to bruise him; he hath put him to grief: when thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed, he shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of the Lord shall prosper in his hand.”

His soul was made a sin offering. It pleased the Lord to bruise him, and they pierced his hands and feet as they did to Christ. Because he was already dead, none of his bones were broken, so the prophecy that he could tell all his bones was fulfilled.

And it did not end in the dust of death: he shall see his seed and prolong his days, and the pleasure of the Lord shall prosper in his hand.

precepts.text: Who hath believed our report, and to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed? He is despised and rejected of men, a man of sorrows; the arm of the Lord is Christ, the power and salvation of the Lord.
precepts.point: A seed shall serve him; it shall be accounted to the Lord for a generation; they shall come and declare his righteousness unto a people that shall be born, that he hath done this. This answers the question Isaiah asked about who shall declare his generation.

note.label: Psalm 22: The Prophecy of Christ on the Cross

precepts.why:
“A seed shall serve him; it shall be accounted to the Lord for a generation.” Isaiah opens with the question this answers: “Who hath believed our report? and to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed?” The arm of the Lord is Christ, the power and salvation of the Lord.

“For he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him. He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not.”

Despised and rejected of men, a man of sorrows, not esteemed. That is the one in Psalm 22 whom the dogs compassed. Yet a seed shall serve him, and they shall come and declare his righteousness unto a people that shall be born.

precepts.text: He was taken from prison and from judgment, and who shall declare his generation? For he was cut off out of the land of the living for the transgression of my people; the seed serving him and accounted for a generation answers that question.
precepts.point: A seed shall serve him; it shall be accounted to the Lord for a generation; they shall come and declare his righteousness unto a people that shall be born, that he hath done this. This answers the question Isaiah asked about who shall declare his generation.

note.label: Psalm 22: The Prophecy of Christ on the Cross

precepts.why:
“He was taken from prison and from judgment: and who shall declare his generation? for he was cut off out of the land of the living: for the transgression of my people was he stricken.” He was cut off out of the land of the living, stricken for the transgression of his people, and Isaiah asks who shall declare his generation.

Psalm 22:30-31 answers that question: “A seed shall serve him; it shall be accounted to the Lord for a generation. They shall come, and shall declare his righteousness unto a people that shall be born, that he hath done this.” The seed that serves him is accounted for a generation, and they declare his righteousness to a people yet to be born.

precepts.text: The one offering of Christ's body that takes away sin and fulfills the sacrifices of the law ties in exactly with this chapter.
precepts.point: This whole chapter is the sacrifice that Christ made, why he made it, what he went through, and the fact that he bore our sins. He poured out his soul unto death, was numbered with the transgressors, bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

note.label: Isaiah 53: The Suffering Servant Bears Our Sins

precepts.why:
This whole chapter is the sacrifice that Christ made, why he made it, what he went through, and the fact that he bore our sins. Hebrews 10 ties in exactly. “For the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things, can never with those sacrifices which they offered year by year continually make the comers thereunto perfect.” “For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins.” In those sacrifices “there is a remembrance again made of sins every year.”

So “when he cometh into the world, he saith, Sacrifice and offering thou wouldest not, but a body hast thou prepared me”. “Then said I, Lo, I come (in the volume of the book it is written of me,) to do thy will, O God.” That prepared body is the one brought “as a lamb to the slaughter”, that “made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death; because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth.” It pleased the Lord to bruise him and make “his soul an offering for sin”.

“He taketh away the first, that he may establish the second. By the which will we are sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.” The one offering of Christ’s body takes away sin and fulfils the sacrifices of the law that could never take it away. He “bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors”, and “by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many; for he shall bear their iniquities.”

precepts.text: Despised and rejected of men, wounded for our transgressions.
precepts.point: What he came to fulfil is the prophecies written concerning him, not the commandments given to Israel to keep. Everything in chapter 2 of this same gospel is an example of that fulfilling.

note.label: Matthew 5: The Sermon on the Mount and the Magnifying of the Law

precepts.why:
The prophets wrote of his suffering: “He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not.”

“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.” This is what Paul meant when he said the prophets and Moses said Christ should suffer. Christ fulfilled Isaiah by being despised and rejected and wounded for our transgressions. That is fulfilling the prophets.

precepts.text: It pleased the Most High to bruise him and make his soul an offering for sin, so that by his knowledge his righteous servant would justify "many," and he bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors.
precepts.point: If you claim Christ suffered and died for all nations, prove it "by the mouth of all his prophets." Show it through Isaiah, Ezekiel, Jeremiah, or Haggai, that Christ suffered and died for all nations, because the text says all his prophets foretold it.

note.label: Acts 3: The Restitution of All Things

precepts.why:
Peter says the Most High showed by the mouth of all his prophets that Christ should suffer, and Isaiah is one of those mouths: “Yet it pleased the Lord to bruise him; he hath put him to grief: when thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed”. His soul made an offering for sin; “he hath poured out his soul unto death: and he was numbered with the transgressors”.

Notice who it is for: “by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many; for he shall bear their iniquities”, and “he bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.” Many, not all nations.

If you claim Christ suffered and died for all nations, prove it by the mouth of all his prophets. Show it through Isaiah, Ezekiel, Jeremiah or Haggai, because the text says all his prophets foretold it. Isaiah foretold a suffering for the many, and the many are defined in the same book.

precepts.text: It pleased the Most High to make His soul an offering for sin.
precepts.point: Christ did only what the Most High intended, to make His soul an offering for sin. The scripture always shows that sacrifice was temporary and that obedience and mercy were desired above it.

note.label: Acts 6: The Grecians Were Greek-Speaking Israelites

precepts.why:
“Yet it pleased the Lord to bruise him; he hath put him to grief: when thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin”. Christ did only what the Most High intended: to make his soul an offering for sin. That is what took the place of the sacrifice and offerings.

This was written in the prophets long before, so Christ did not come to destroy the law or the prophets. The sacrifice was set aside according to the scripture, not against it, and the false witnesses had no case.
